chunks: High-current layout rules of thumb. The question: What are some rules of thumb when laying out and routing high-current connections?
Copper is not a perfect wire. It has resistance, so a trace carrying lots of current gets warm and loses voltage.
For high-current paths you keep the copper short and wide, use pours or planes where you can, and watch the weak spots: vias, narrow necks at pads, and connectors.
Route the return path as carefully as the supply.
Picture a garden hose carrying lots of water. A short, wide hose delivers it with little pressure lost. A long, thin one loses pressure along the way.
A kink or narrow fitting is where the flow struggles most. The return path is a drain that must be just as wide.
The width needed grows faster than linearly with current, and halving the allowed temperature rise costs you a lot of copper (10 amps needs about 7.
2 mm for 10 degrees Celsius but only 3. 1 mm for 40 degrees Celsius). Note how a trace sized for 5 amps cannot simply be doubled in width to carry 10 amps.
Squares: a trace's length divided by its width. A trace 1 mm wide and 50 mm long is 50 squares. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square of copper, whatever its size.
About 0. 48 milliohms for 1 oz copper. Copper weight (oz): the copper thickness. 1 oz is about 35 µm.
IR drop: the voltage I times R lost in the wiring ("Why the supply goes close to the load"). Via array: several vias in parallel on one net, sharing the current.
A trace 1 mm wide and 50 mm long is 50 squares, so 50 times 0. 48 equals 24 milliohms. At 10 amps it loses 10 times 0. 024 equals 0. 24 volts and turns 10 squared times 0.
024 equals 2. 4 watts into heat in a tiny strip. Widen it to 6 mm and it is about 8 squares: 4 milliohms, 40 millivolts and 0. 4 watts. That is the whole idea.
"I treat copper as a resistor: about 0. 5 milliohms per square for 1 oz.
So I keep high-current paths short and wide, use pours or planes, size the width from an IPC temperature-rise chart and then check the voltage drop separately.
I use several vias in parallel, avoid necking down at pads, and route the return path as carefully as the supply. Then I verify with a thermal camera on the first board."
